The sky is blue because of a phenomenon called **Rayleigh scattering**. 

Light from the sun looks white, but it's actually made up of all the colors of the rainbow. These colors travel in waves. Red light has long, lazy waves, while blue and violet light have short, choppy waves. 

When sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere, it crashes into the gases and particles in the air (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). The longer wavelengths, like red and yellow, mostly pass straight through without hitting much. But the shorter wavelengths, like blue, hit the gas molecules and scatter in every direction across the sky. When you look up, you are seeing this scattered blue light.

**Why not violet?**
Violet light actually has an even shorter wavelength than blue, so it gets scattered even more! We should theoretically see a violet sky. However, the sun emits much less violet light than blue light to begin with. More importantly, our eyes are biologically much more sensitive to blue light than violet light. So, our brains interpret the sky as blue.

**Everyday connection:**
You can see a similar effect when looking at smoke from a campfire or a cigarette against a dark background; the smoke often appears slightly blue because the tiny particles scatter the short blue light waves from the ambient light, just like the atmosphere does with sunlight.
